title: Modal Logic and Possible Worlds
subtitle: The logic of 'must', 'might' and 'what would have happened if'
objectives: By the end you will be able to distinguish several kinds of modality (logical, metaphysical, physical, epistemic, deontic).
By the end you will be able to use the symbols □ and ◇ and explain their duality.
By the end you will be able to evaluate modal sentences in a small possible-worlds model and explain the role of the accessibility relation.
By the end you will be able to explain Kripke's rigid designators and the idea of necessary truths known a posteriori.
By the end you will be able to state the Stalnaker–Lewis analysis of counterfactuals and compare modal realism with its rivals.
hook:
You missed your train by thirty seconds. You stand on the platform thinking: if I hadn't stopped for coffee, I would have caught it. That thought is about something that did not happen. Yet it seems plainly true, and its rival ("if I hadn't stopped for coffee, I would have missed it anyway") seems plainly false. What makes a claim about a non-existent situation true or false?

Our reasoning is soaked in such words: *must*, *might*, *could have*, *necessarily*, *possibly*, *would have*. Propositional and predicate logic (Lessons 1 and 2) cannot handle them, because "necessarily P" is not a truth function of P: some true statements are necessary (2 + 2 = 4) and others are not (you missed your train). **Modal logic** is the logic of these words. Its central tool, the idea of possible worlds, began as a metaphor in Leibniz (Day 46) and became, in the twentieth century, one of the most productive and controversial ideas in philosophy.

sections.heading: Kinds of Necessity and the Box and Diamond
sections.body:
A statement's **modality** is the way in which it is true or false: necessarily, possibly, contingently. A **necessary** truth could not have been false. A **possible** statement could be true (whether or not it is). A **contingent** statement is true but could have been false, or false but could have been true.

But "could" has many senses:
- **Logical** necessity: true by logic alone. "Either it's raining or it isn't."
- **Metaphysical** necessity: true in every way the world could really have been. Many philosophers think "Water is H₂O" is metaphysically necessary, though not a truth of logic.
- **Physical** (or nomological) necessity: required by the laws of nature. "Nothing travels faster than light" is physically necessary but, presumably, the laws could have been different.
- **Epistemic** modality: about what is compatible with what we know. "The keys might be in the car" means nothing I know rules it out.
- **Deontic** modality: about obligation and permission. "You must pay your taxes" says what is required, not what will happen.

Modal logic writes "necessarily P" as □P (the box) and "possibly P" as ◇P (the diamond). The two are **duals**, linked by negation just as ∀ and ∃ were in Lesson 2:
- □P is equivalent to ¬◇¬P: necessarily P means it is not possible that not-P.
- ◇P is equivalent to ¬□¬P: possibly P means it is not necessary that not-P.

The resemblance to the quantifiers is no accident, as you will see in a moment.

Modal reasoning is ancient. In *On Interpretation*, chapter 9, Aristotle (Day 17) puzzled over whether it is *now* true or false that there will be a sea battle tomorrow; if it is already true, the battle seems necessary, and the future seems fixed. Medieval logicians developed modal syllogistics. The modern subject begins with C. I. Lewis, who, troubled by the paradoxes of the material conditional you met in Lesson 1, proposed a **strict implication**: P strictly implies Q when it is *necessary* that P → Q. In *Symbolic Logic* (1932, with C. H. Langford) he set out several modal systems, S1 to S5, with different axioms. But it was not clear what the axioms meant or which was correct, until possible worlds semantics arrived.

sections.heading: Possible Worlds Semantics
sections.body:
Leibniz had described God choosing the best among infinitely many possible worlds. In the late 1950s and early 1960s, several logicians, most influentially the teenage Saul Kripke (whose first paper on the topic appeared in 1959, when he was 18), along with Stig Kanger and Jaakko Hintikka, turned this idea into precise mathematics.

The idea: a **possible world** is a complete way things could be. Then:
- □P is true at a world w if P is true at every world possible relative to w.
- ◇P is true at a world w if P is true at at least one world possible relative to w.

So the box is a universal quantifier over worlds and the diamond an existential one. That explains the duality.

What does "possible relative to w" mean? Kripke introduced an **accessibility relation**: a world v is accessible from w if v is a genuine possibility from w's point of view. Different kinds of modality correspond to different accessibility relations. For physical necessity, the accessible worlds are those with the same laws of nature; for epistemic modality, the worlds compatible with what you know.

A worked example. Take three worlds, w1, w2 and w3, each accessible from every other and from itself. Let P ("It is raining") be true at w1 and w2 but false at w3. Let Q ("2 + 2 = 4") be true at all three. Now evaluate at w1:
- P is true at w1.
- □P is false at w1, since P fails at the accessible world w3.
- ◇¬P is true at w1, since w3 is an accessible world where P fails.
- □Q is true at w1, since Q holds at every accessible world.
- So P is *contingent*: true, but not necessarily true.

The beauty of the semantics is that the old axioms now correspond to properties of the accessibility relation:
- Axiom T, □P → P (what is necessary is true), holds when every world can access itself (the relation is **reflexive**).
- Axiom 4, □P → □□P, holds when accessibility is **transitive**.
- Axiom 5, ◇P → □◇P, holds when it is **Euclidean** (if w sees u and v, then u sees v).
- **S5**, the system most philosophers use for metaphysical necessity, has an accessibility relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive: every world sees every world in its group.

This also explains why different modalities need different logics. In deontic logic, read □P as "P is obligatory." Then axiom T fails: it ought to be that nobody steals, but people do. So deontic logic uses a relation that is not reflexive: the accessible worlds are the morally ideal ones, and ours is not among them.

sections.heading: Kripke: Naming, Necessity and the A Posteriori
sections.body:
Possible worlds also transformed the philosophy of language. In three lectures given at Princeton in 1970, published as *Naming and Necessity* (1980), Kripke argued for several surprising theses.

First, distinguish two readings of modal sentences. Quine's example: "The number of planets is necessarily greater than 7." (When he wrote, the count was 9; we now count 8.) Read **de dicto** ("about the saying"), it says that the sentence "the number of planets is greater than 7" is necessarily true, which is false: there could have been just 5 planets. Read **de re** ("about the thing"), it says that the number that actually counts the planets, 8, is necessarily greater than 7, which is true. Formally this is a scope difference, like those in Lesson 2: does □ sit outside or inside the description?

Second, Kripke argued that ordinary proper names are **rigid designators**: they pick out the same object in every possible world where it exists. "Aristotle" refers to that very man even when we describe worlds in which he never taught Alexander or became a philosopher. Descriptions like "the teacher of Alexander" are usually not rigid: in another world someone else could have taught Alexander. This was an attack on the description theory of names associated with Frege and Russell (Day 69).

Third, and most strikingly, there are **necessary a posteriori** truths. Ancient astronomers named the bright morning star *Phosphorus* and the evening star *Hesperus*, and later discovered both are the planet Venus. Since both names rigidly designate Venus, "Hesperus is Phosphorus" is true in every world where Venus exists: it is necessary. Yet it was discovered by observation, not by reflection. Likewise, Kripke argued, "Water is H₂O" is necessary but known a posteriori.

This broke a link that had seemed obvious since Hume's fork (Day 49) and Kant (Day 55): that necessity goes with a priori knowledge and contingency with experience. Kripke separated metaphysics (necessary or contingent?) from epistemology (known a priori or a posteriori?). The idea has been hugely influential, though philosophers continue to debate whether the necessity of "water is H₂O" is as secure as Kripke claimed.

sections.heading: What Are Possible Worlds, Really?
sections.body:
If modal truths are truths about possible worlds, what are these worlds? Here philosophers split sharply.

**Modal realism.** David Lewis, in *On the Plurality of Worlds* (1986), defended the view that possible worlds are as real as ours: concrete universes, spatiotemporally disconnected from us, with their own donkeys, planets and people. "Actual" just means "this one, the one we are in," much as "here" means the place where the speaker is. Lewis's argument was a cost-benefit one: positing these worlds gives a unified, reductive account of possibility, counterfactuals, properties and propositions, and he thought this theoretical payoff was worth the ontological price. He admitted that his view met with what he called "the incredulous stare" and conceded that he could not refute a stare.

Lewis added that individuals do not exist in more than one world. Instead, you have **counterparts** in other worlds: people very similar to you. "You could have been a pianist" is true because some counterpart of yours is a pianist. Kripke objected with what is called the Humphrey objection: when we say that Hubert Humphrey (who lost the 1968 US presidential election) might have won, we are talking about Humphrey himself, and Humphrey could not care less whether someone else, however similar, wins in another universe.

**Actualism.** Most philosophers reject Lewis's realism and hold that only the actual world exists. Possible worlds are then abstract objects that exist here: for example, maximal consistent sets of propositions (Robert Adams), or ways the world could have been, conceived as properties the universe might have had (Robert Stalnaker), or maximal possible states of affairs (Alvin Plantinga). These are often called **ersatz** worlds. The challenge for ersatzism is to explain what makes a set of propositions "consistent" or "possible" without going in a circle, since possibility is what we were trying to explain.

Kripke himself took a deflationary line: possible worlds are not distant countries we discover with telescopes but situations we *stipulate*. When we ask what would have happened if Nixon had lost, we begin with Nixon and describe a scenario about him. On this view, possible worlds are a useful bookkeeping device, not a new ontology.

sections.heading: Counterfactuals: The Logic of 'Would Have'
sections.body:
Return to the missed train. A **counterfactual** is a conditional whose antecedent is (presumed) false: "If I hadn't stopped for coffee, I would have caught the train." In Lesson 1 we saw that the material conditional cannot handle these; every material conditional with a false antecedent is true, so it would make "If I hadn't stopped, I would have missed it anyway" true as well.

The strict conditional does no better. It is not *necessary* that if I skip coffee I catch the train: in some possible worlds the train is cancelled, or I trip on the stairs. We want to ignore those far-fetched worlds.

Robert Stalnaker (1968) and David Lewis (*Counterfactuals*, 1973) proposed the now-standard answer: a counterfactual "If A had been the case, C would have been the case" is true when, in the possible worlds **most similar** to the actual world in which A is true, C is also true. (Stalnaker assumed there is a single closest A-world; Lewis allowed ties.) In the closest worlds where I skip coffee, everything else stays roughly the same: the train leaves on time, I walk at my usual pace, and I catch it.

This analysis explains a striking feature: counterfactuals are **non-monotonic**. In ordinary logic, if "If A then C" holds, so does "If A and B, then C." Not so with counterfactuals:
- If I had struck this match, it would have lit. (True.)
- If I had struck this match and it had been soaked in water, it would have lit. (False.)

The closest worlds where the match is struck are dry-match worlds; the closest worlds where it is struck and soaked are different worlds. Lewis's own example: "If kangaroos had no tails, they would topple over"; but add "and used crutches," and the conditional changes.

The hard part is **similarity**. Which worlds count as closest? If Nixon had pressed the nuclear button (an example from Kit Fine's critique), the closest world might seem to be one where a small miracle stopped the missiles, since a world with nuclear war is enormously different from ours. Lewis replied with a detailed ranking that weights avoiding big violations of law and keeping exact match of past history, and the debate continues. The stakes are high, because counterfactuals are central to accounts of causation (Lewis analyzed "c caused e" roughly as "if c had not happened, e would not have happened"), of free will ("could have done otherwise," which the Mind track will examine), and of moral and legal responsibility.

keyQuote.text: Possible worlds are stipulated, not discovered by powerful telescopes.
keyQuote.source: Saul Kripke, Naming and Necessity (1980), Lecture I

modernConnection.title: Counterfactual Explanations and Machines That Check Every Future
modernConnection.body:
Suppose a bank's algorithm rejects your loan application. You ask why. One proposal, made influential by Sandra Wachter, Brent Mittelstadt and Chris Russell in a 2017 paper, is that the system should give you a **counterfactual explanation**: "If your annual income had been $5,000 higher, your loan would have been approved." This tells you what to change without requiring the bank to reveal the whole model. It is precisely the Stalnaker–Lewis idea put to work: find the *closest* possible world (the smallest change to your data) in which the outcome differs.

The analogy also reveals the old philosophical problem in new clothes. What counts as closest? Changing your income by $5,000 might be "smaller" numerically than changing your age by one year, but you can do something about one and not the other. And if the model uses features correlated with race or gender, counterfactual questions such as "Would you have been approved if you were a different race?" raise exactly the puzzles of identity across worlds that divided Kripke and Lewis: which of your other features stay fixed when we imagine that change? Computer scientists working on algorithmic fairness, drawing on Judea Pearl's mathematical theory of causation, now argue about these questions in technical journals.

Modal logic also runs quietly inside the software that checks safety-critical systems. In 1977 Amir Pnueli proposed using **temporal logic**, a modal logic in which □ means "at every future time" and ◇ means "at some future time," to specify the behavior of programs. "□(request → ◇response)" says that every request is eventually answered. Pnueli received the Turing Award in 1996 for this work, and **model checking** tools now explore the possible states of chip designs, aircraft software and communication protocols to verify such properties. Here possible worlds are literal: the states a machine could reach. Whether the worlds of metaphysics are like that is, as we saw, another question.

vocabulary.definition: The logic of necessity, possibility and related notions, using operators such as □ (necessarily) and ◇ (possibly).
vocabulary.example: Modal logic lets us distinguish 'it is raining' from 'it must be raining'.

vocabulary.definition: A complete way things could have been; used to give the meaning of modal statements.
vocabulary.example: There is a possible world in which you were born in a different century.

vocabulary.definition: In Kripke semantics, the relation that says which worlds count as possible relative to a given world.
vocabulary.example: For physical necessity, only worlds with our laws of nature are accessible.

vocabulary.definition: True but possibly false, or false but possibly true; neither necessary nor impossible.
vocabulary.example: That the Eiffel Tower is in Paris is contingent: it could have been built in Lyon.

vocabulary.definition: An expression that refers to the same object in every possible world in which that object exists.
vocabulary.example: 'Venus' is a rigid designator, but 'the second planet from the Sun' is not.

vocabulary.definition: A truth that could not have been false but can only be known through experience.
vocabulary.example: Kripke held that 'Hesperus is Phosphorus' is necessary a posteriori.

vocabulary.definition: Two readings of a modal claim: about a thing itself (de re) or about a statement or description (de dicto).
vocabulary.example: 'The president must be a citizen' is true de dicto but not de re about the person who happens to be president.

vocabulary.definition: A conditional about what would have been the case if something that did not happen had happened.
vocabulary.example: 'If the asteroid had missed, dinosaurs might still rule the Earth' is a counterfactual.

thinkingExercise.title: Build a Tiny Model and Test a Counterfactual
thinkingExercise.prompt: Practice possible worlds reasoning on a decision from your own life.
steps: Pick a moment where things could have gone otherwise (a job you didn't take, a city you didn't move to). Write one counterfactual you believe about it, of the form 'If I had A, then C would have happened.'
Describe the closest possible world in which A is true: what changes, and, just as important, what stays the same?
Add an extra condition B to the antecedent that would make the counterfactual false, to see non-monotonicity in action.
Now draw three possible worlds on paper with arrows for accessibility, label which simple statements are true in each, and evaluate one □ statement and one ◇ statement at your actual world.

Reflect: when you think about what 'could have' happened, do you believe the other possibilities are in any sense real? Which view of possible worlds (Lewis, ersatzism, Kripke's stipulation) best fits your answer?

summary: Modality comes in many kinds (logical, metaphysical, physical, epistemic, deontic); modal logic writes 'necessarily' as □ and 'possibly' as ◇, and each is the dual of the other.
Kripke semantics treats □ as 'true in all accessible worlds' and ◇ as 'true in some accessible world'; properties of the accessibility relation correspond to axioms like T, 4 and 5.
Kripke argued that names are rigid designators and that some truths, like 'Hesperus is Phosphorus', are necessary yet known a posteriori, separating metaphysics from epistemology.
David Lewis held that possible worlds are concrete and real (modal realism with counterparts); most philosophers prefer abstract 'ersatz' worlds or Kripke's view that worlds are stipulated.
On the Stalnaker–Lewis analysis, counterfactuals are true when the consequent holds in the most similar antecedent-worlds; this makes them non-monotonic, and the notion of similarity remains debated.

quiz.question: Which is equivalent to □P ('necessarily P')?
quiz.explanation: Necessarily P means it is not possible that not-P. Box and diamond are duals, like ∀ and ∃.

quiz.question: In Kripke semantics, when is ◇P true at a world w?
options: When P is true at w
When P is true at every world
When P is true at some world accessible from w
When P is true at no world accessible from w
quiz.explanation: The diamond is an existential quantifier over accessible worlds: P holds in at least one of them.

quiz.question: In deontic logic, where □P means 'P is obligatory', the axiom □P → P should be rejected.
quiz.explanation: What ought to be the case often is not: it is obligatory that nobody steals, yet people steal. So deontic logic drops axiom T by using an accessibility relation that is not reflexive.

quiz.question: Kripke argued that 'Hesperus is Phosphorus' is:
quiz.explanation: Both names rigidly designate Venus, so the identity holds in every world where Venus exists, yet it was discovered by astronomical observation.

quiz.question: What is a rigid designator?
options: An expression that refers to the same object in every possible world where it exists
A description that applies to only one thing
A name that cannot be translated
quiz.explanation: Kripke held that proper names are rigid, unlike most descriptions such as 'the teacher of Alexander', which could pick out different people in different worlds.

quiz.question: 'If I had struck the match, it would have lit' is true, but 'If I had struck the match and it had been wet, it would have lit' is false. This shows that counterfactuals are:
quiz.explanation: Adding information to the antecedent can turn a true counterfactual false, because it changes which worlds are the closest.

quiz.question: David Lewis held that other possible worlds are concrete universes just as real as our own.
quiz.explanation: That is modal realism. For Lewis, 'actual' simply means 'the world we are in', and individuals have counterparts in other worlds rather than existing in many worlds.

quiz.question: A loan system tells an applicant: 'If your savings had been $2,000 higher, you would have been approved.' Which philosophical idea does this most directly apply?
quiz.explanation: Counterfactual explanations search for the most similar alternative situation in which the outcome changes, which is the Stalnaker–Lewis idea.

quiz.question: Kripke's Humphrey objection says that counterpart theory changes the subject: when we say Humphrey might have won, we mean Humphrey himself, not someone similar in another world.
quiz.explanation: Kripke argued that Humphrey would not care whether someone else, however similar, won in another universe, so counterparts seem the wrong thing for our claim to be about.

goDeeper.body:
Modal logic has given new life to an old argument. On Day 34 you met Anselm's ontological argument. Alvin Plantinga, in *The Nature of Necessity* (1974), offered a modal version. Define a maximally great being as one that has maximal excellence (omnipotence, omniscience, moral perfection) in every possible world. The argument runs: (1) It is possible that a maximally great being exists: ◇□G. (2) In S5, ◇□G implies □G. (3) So a maximally great being exists necessarily, and therefore actually. Step (2) is a genuine theorem of S5, which follows from the Euclidean property of accessibility. So the argument is valid in S5.

The debate therefore shifts to premise (1). Critics point out a symmetry: it seems just as possible that there is *no* maximally great being, ◇¬G. But ◇¬G implies ¬□G, and in S5 that implies ¬◇□G, which contradicts premise (1). So the possibility premise is not innocent: in S5, saying a necessary being is possible is equivalent to saying it is actual. Plantinga himself conceded that the argument does not prove God's existence to someone who rejects the premise, while maintaining that it shows the belief can be rational.

This example illustrates a lesson from Lesson 1 that becomes vivid in modal logic: validity is cheap; all the action is in the premises. It also shows why the choice of modal system is not merely technical. Whether S5 is the right logic for metaphysical necessity is itself a philosophical question, and some, like Nathan Salmon, have argued against it. Timothy Williamson's *Modal Logic as Metaphysics* (2013) goes further, defending the controversial view that everything necessarily exists, with striking consequences for what possible worlds contain.

questions: Can we know what is possible by imagining it? If you can imagine water not being H₂O, does that show it could have been otherwise?
Is Lewis's modal realism a reductio of possible worlds talk, or the honest price of taking it seriously?
Should an AI system's counterfactual explanations be allowed to mention features you cannot change, like your age or birthplace?
